kurz: Which four deductions lie between revenue and net profit, and which assumption is built into every ratio that leaves out one of these levels.

bloecke.md:
The balance sheet shows the position on a reporting date, the income statement (Gewinn- und Verlustrechnung, GuV) the development over twelve months. It shows what is left of revenue once all the expenses of the period have been set against it.

The income statement allocates income and expenses to the period to which they economically belong. Revenue is recognised when the goods or services have been delivered, not only when the money comes in. Depreciation and the creation of provisions reduce profit without anything being paid out. The income statement therefore measures economic performance and not liquidity. A company can report profits and still become insolvent if the money is tied up in inventories, receivables and investments. Only the cash flow statement shows the payments.

## Nature of expense method and cost of sales method

Section 275 HGB (Commercial Code) prescribes the vertical format and permits two layouts. The **nature of expense method** (Gesamtkostenverfahren, subsection 2) classifies expenses by type (materials, personnel, depreciation, other operating expenses). It works with the total output of the period. The items “change in inventories” and “other own work capitalised” therefore take account of what was produced but not sold. The **cost of sales method** (Umsatzkostenverfahren, subsection 3) classifies by function (production, selling, administration) and sets against revenue only the costs of the goods and services sold in the period.

Net profit is the same under both methods, while the items above it differ. Gross profit is a mandatory item only under the cost of sales method. Under the nature of expense method, the gross margin can only be estimated approximately from the cost of materials, and when two companies are compared, this estimate should be disclosed. Conversely, under the cost of sales method the personnel expense ratio cannot be read from the income statement, because wages are spread across three functions. Depreciation does not appear there as a separate item either. To calculate EBITDA from financial statements prepared under the cost of sales method, you therefore need the notes or the cash flow statement. Capital-market-oriented groups report under IFRS, which also permits both layouts. Industrial groups more often choose the cost of sales method, utilities and many service providers more often the nature of expense method.

bloecke.md:
## Profit levels between revenue and net profit

Between revenue and net profit lie four blocks: the cost of the goods and services provided, capital consumption, financing and taxes. The usual intermediate figures sit at these transitions but are not governed by law. Neither [[EBITDA]] nor EBIT is defined in IFRS or in the HGB. Each company calculates them itself and calls the result operating result, operating profit, EBIT or adjusted EBITDA. The same names do not necessarily mean the same thing. What matters more than the figure on the front page of the investor presentation is therefore the reconciliation in the notes, which shows how the figure was derived.

bloecke.formel:
Net profit + income taxes = EBT
EBT + net interest expense = EBIT
EBIT + depreciation and amortisation = EBITDA
bloecke.erklaerung: The calculation starts at the bottom with net profit, because only that figure is defined by law. Each step upwards strips out another type of cost: first taxes, then the cost of financing and finally the wearing out of fixed assets.
variablen: earnings before interest and taxes, that is, operating performance regardless of financing
earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation and amortisation of tangible and intangible fixed assets
bloecke.beispiel: For the model company below, all figures in € million: 94.5 + 40.5 = 135 (EBT); 135 + 25 = 160 (EBIT); 160 + 75 = 235 (EBITDA).

bloecke.titel: Mechanical engineering company with €1 billion revenue
bloecke.md:
Cost of sales method, amounts in € million, income tax rate 30%; the figures are constructed but internally consistent. Revenue 1,000 − cost of sales 620 = gross profit 380; − selling 130 − administration 70 − net other items 20 = EBIT 160; − net interest expense 25 = EBT 135; − taxes 40.5 = net profit 94.5. The costs down to EBIT include depreciation and amortisation of 75, so EBITDA is 235.

The €75 million of depreciation and amortisation does not appear anywhere in the layout as a separate item. It is spread across the three functions and only becomes visible in the notes and in the cash flow statement.

bloecke.md:
## What each profit level tells you

The **gross margin** of 38% shows what is left when only the cost of the goods and services sold has been deducted. For competitive strength it is the most informative level, because it comes before all structural and financing decisions. Under price pressure, it is usually the first to give way.

Between EBITDA and EBIT lie €75 million of depreciation and amortisation. They spread the cost of the machines used to generate the revenue over their useful life and are therefore costs of the ongoing business. A ratio that leaves them out assumes that the assets do not need to be replaced.

Between EBIT and EBT, the financing structure costs €25 million. This level tells you about the balance sheet, not about operating quality. That is why businesses are compared on EBIT and not on net profit. Two identical factories, one debt-free and one debt-financed, have the same EBIT but very different net margins.

Between EBT and net profit lie taxes. The **net margin** of 9.5% is therefore the level that depends most on influences outside the operating business. At the same time, net profit is the figure from which earnings per share are derived.

Corporations (Kapitalgesellschaften) pay corporation tax of 15% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it, together 15.825%. In addition there is trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), which is calculated as the base rate (Steuermesszahl) of 3.5% multiplied by the municipal multiplier (Hebesatz). The multiplier is at least 200%, and from 2027 at least 280%, which corresponds to 7% and 9.8% trade tax. In municipalities with at least 20,000 inhabitants, multipliers in 2025 ranged between 250% and 580%. That means about 8.75% to 20.3% trade tax and a total burden of roughly 24.6% to 36.1%. Berlin is at about 30%, Frankfurt at about 32% and Munich at about 33%. Since July 2025, the law has provided that corporation tax will fall in stages, to 14% from 2028 and then by one percentage point a year to 10% from 2032 (Section 23 of the Corporation Tax Act, KStG).

The tax rate reported in the consolidated financial statements regularly deviates from this, because foreign subsidiaries, loss carryforwards and deferred taxes affect it. A group tax rate that remains conspicuously low over the long term should not be seen as an achievement of management. It raises the question of whether the profit is sustainable.

## Purpose and limits of EBITDA

EBITDA has a legitimate purpose. It makes two companies comparable that differ in debt, depreciation policy and tax domicile. It is also the usual reference figure in loan agreements. The leverage ratio, that is, net financial debt divided by EBITDA, can be read as the number of years a company would need to repay its debt if nothing gets in the way.

On the other hand, the ratio assumes that depreciation is not a real expense. For a software company with few fixed assets, that is roughly true. For an airline, a network operator or a semiconductor plant it is grossly wrong, because there depreciation is the cost of the assets on which the business model rests. In addition, because EBITDA is not defined in any standard, each company decides for itself what to include.

bloecke.text: References to EBITDA make us shudder.
bloecke.quelle: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, shareholder letter 2000

bloecke.md: Buffett then asks whether management thinks the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures. His objection is to the use of the ratio as a substitute for profit, not to the ratio itself.

bloecke.md: Since 2019, rental agreements have been accounted for under IFRS 16 like purchases on credit. What previously reduced EBITDA as rental expense now appears as depreciation and interest expense, that is, below EBITDA. For retailers, airlines and restaurant chains, EBITDA rises significantly as a result, without anything having changed in the business. At the same time, reported net debt increases by the lease liabilities. When comparing time series across 2019, or HGB with IFRS financial statements, both effects must therefore be adjusted for. Without this adjustment, the differences mainly show the effect of the accounting rules.

## Margins across sectors

A net margin of 1.3% looks like a bad business but is normal in food retail. There, capital is turned over several times a year, so the thin margin becomes a decent return on capital. Conversely, a gross margin of over 70% at a software company says nothing about whether anything is left after selling, research and share-based payment.

The following figures come from Damodaran's analysis of just under 6,000 US companies, with data as of January 2026. The market as a whole has a gross margin of 37.76%, an EBITDA margin of 16.56% and a net margin of 9.74%. Banks appear in such tables with a gross margin of almost 100%, because their interest expense does not count as cost of sales. This is a result of the layout and not an advantage. In Germany, the figures tend to be lower because of a different sector mix and a higher tax burden, but the ranking of the sectors is similar.

bloecke.md: Utilities and telecoms achieve almost the same EBITDA margin as software companies but lose about three-fifths of it on the way to the net margin. The EBITDA margin shows earning power before depreciation and amortisation, interest and taxes, the net margin the share that remains after all costs.

## Special items and adjusted figures

Only what happens once should count as one-off. Restructuring expenses, litigation, goodwill impairments and integration costs are legitimate adjustments in themselves, but only if they are out of the ordinary. If a group adjusts for restructuring expenses five years in a row, it is restructuring permanently, and the costs belong to the ongoing business.

In the regulatory framework, such figures are called alternative performance measures. The ESMA guidelines have applied since 3 July 2016. For each of these figures they require a clear definition, a reconciliation to the closest IFRS figure, an explanation of its usefulness, comparative figures for the previous year, consistent application over time and no greater prominence than the IFRS figure. The practical check takes ten minutes. You add up the adjustments over five years and compare the total with the cumulative IFRS result for the same five years. If the adjustments are of the same order of magnitude, the adjusted figure no longer corrects exceptions and mainly reflects management's presentation.

IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 and applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. It is the first standard to prescribe the structure of the income statement. It requires mandatory categories for income and expenses and the mandatory subtotals “operating profit” and “profit before financing and income taxes”. In addition, management-defined performance measures, that is, the adjusted figures that companies create themselves, must be disclosed and reconciled. This does not yet apply to financial years up to and including 2026. Comparisons across this cut-off date will therefore again require adjustment.

## Earnings per share

IAS 33 applies to companies whose shares are publicly traded and requires two figures of equal rank: basic and diluted earnings per share. The numerator is the profit attributable to the ordinary shareholders of the parent company. Non-controlling interests and preference dividends are therefore deducted. The denominator is the **weighted average** number of shares. Because of the weighting, a capital increase in the middle of the year counts for only half. Otherwise a whole year's profit would be spread over shares that have only existed since July.

Diluted earnings are calculated as if all dilutive rights to shares had already been exercised. For options, the treasury stock method applies. It assumes that the exercise proceeds are used to buy back the company's own shares at the average price, so that only the excess increases the number of shares. Convertible bonds increase the denominator by the conversion shares and the numerator by the after-tax interest that is then saved. Rights that would increase earnings per share are disregarded. Diluted earnings per share are therefore by definition never higher than basic earnings per share.

bloecke.formel: EPS = (net profit − non-controlling interests − preference dividends) / weighted average number of shares
bloecke.erklaerung: For diluted earnings, the numerator is increased by the after-tax interest saved on convertible instruments and the denominator by all dilutive potential shares.
variablen: shares outstanding, weighted by the fraction of the year in which they were outstanding
exercise proceeds divided by the average price gives the shares notionally bought back
an instrument is dilutive if its incremental earnings per additional share are below the existing EPS

bloecke.md:
The example continues the model company. Of the net profit of €94.5 million, €4.5 million is attributable to non-controlling interests, leaving €90.0 million. On 1 January, 50.0 million shares were outstanding; on 1 July, 6.0 million more were added from a capital increase.

- Weighted number of shares: 50.0 + 6.0 × 6/12 = 53.0 million, which gives EPS = 90.0 / 53.0 = €1.70.
- Using the year-end total of 56.0 million shares would give €1.61, using the opening total €1.80. Both figures would be wrong.
- Options on 3.0 million shares, exercise price €20, average price €32: the proceeds of €60 million notionally buy back €60 million / €32 = 1,875,000 shares, so 1,125,000 shares are added.
- Convertible bond of €100 million with a 2% coupon, convertible into 4.0 million shares: the interest saving of €2.0 million less 30% tax increases earnings by €1.4 million, and the number of shares rises by 4.0 million. That is €0.35 per additional share. This is less than €1.70, so the bond is dilutive and is included.
- Diluted earnings per share: €91.4 million / 58,125,000 shares = €1.57, a decrease of 7.4%.

If profit rises by 5% and the diluted share count by 7%, earnings per share fall. The diluted share count over five to ten years is therefore a time series in its own right that belongs next to the profit series. It is found in the notes and not in the press release. Where dilution comes from, and why share-based payment causes real costs even though nothing is paid out, is covered in a later lesson of this module.

bloecke.titel: Approach to analysing the income statement
bloecke.md:
1. Establish whether the income statement is structured by the cost of sales method or the nature of expense method, and deduce from this which margins can be read off at all.
2. Place five financial years side by side and look at revenue growth separately from the development of margins. If revenue grows while the margin falls, growth comes at the expense of profitability.
3. Find the reconciliation from the adjusted figure to the IFRS figure and add up the adjustments of the last five years.
4. Take depreciation and amortisation from the notes or the cash flow statement and compare them with capital expenditure. If capital expenditure stays below depreciation over the long term, the asset base is shrinking.
5. Look at the diluted share count and net profit together over the years.

Under IAS 38, research costs must be expensed immediately, whereas development costs must be capitalised as soon as the criteria are met. Section 248(2) HGB grants an option for internally generated intangible fixed assets.

Capitalisation has a considerable effect on the income statement. It takes expense out of the current year, increases profit and the balance sheet total today, and burdens the following years with amortisation. It flatters EBITDA twice over, because the expense disappears today and the later amortisation is recorded below EBITDA. Under the nature of expense method, the amount appears visibly as “other own work capitalised”. Under the cost of sales method, it is netted off against cost of sales and can only be found via the statement of changes in fixed assets in the notes. If the capitalisation rate rises while revenue stagnates, you should take a closer look.

mitnehmen: Revenue, gross profit, EBITDA, EBIT, EBT and net profit differ by four types of cost, namely the cost of goods and services provided, capital consumption, financing and taxes.
EBITDA and EBIT are not defined in any accounting standard, so the reconciliation matters more than the reported figure.
The gap between EBITDA margin and net margin depends on the sector and ranges from about 4 points in food retail to over 20 points for utilities and telecoms.
Margins are only comparable within a sector, and with high capital turnover a thin margin can be the better business.

For earnings per share, the weighted and diluted share count is what matters; a capital increase in the middle of the year counts for only half, for options only the excess counts under the treasury stock method, and dilutive convertible bonds are included with all their conversion shares.

begriffe.text: Revenue less the production cost of the goods and services sold. It is a mandatory item only under the cost of sales method under Section 275(3) HGB. The gross margin derived from it measures pricing power.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. The figure is not defined in any accounting standard and is therefore calculated by each company itself. It systematically leaves out the need for reinvestment.

Layout of the income statement by function (production, selling, administration) under Section 275(3) HGB. It shows gross profit but does not report depreciation and personnel expenses as separate items.

A ratio defined by the company itself outside the accounting standards, such as adjusted EBIT. The ESMA guidelines require a definition, a reconciliation to the closest IFRS figure, comparative figures and consistent application.

Earnings per share on the assumption that all dilutive options, convertible bonds and subscription rights have been exercised. Under IAS 33, it must be presented with equal prominence alongside the basic figure.
